segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus’s mother was there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus and his disciples had also been invited to the wedding.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the wine ran out, Jesus’s mother said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have no wine.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What does this have to do with me, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His mother said to the servants,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do whatever he tells you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now six stone water jars were standing there for the purification rites of the Jews, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Fill the jars with water.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they filled them to the brim.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the master of the banquet tasted the water that had become wine—he did not know where it came from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew—he called the bridegroom

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Everyone serves the good wine first, and the lesser wine once the guests are drunk. You have kept the good wine until now.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus did this as the beginning of his signs in Cana of Galilee; he revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the temple courts he found people selling cattle, sheep and doves, and the money changers sitting at their tables.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He made a whip out of cords and drove them all out of the temple courts, sheep and cattle alike; he poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to those selling the doves he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take these out of here! Stop making my Father’s house a house of trade.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples remembered that it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jewish leaders responded and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What sign do you show us, since you are doing these things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jewish leaders then said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and you will raise it in three days?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he was speaking about the temple of his body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the festival, many trusted in his name, seeing the signs he was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, for his part, did not trust himself to them, because he knew everyone

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and because he had no need for anyone to testify about a person, for he himself knew what was in a person.

notes.phrase: What does this have to do with me
notes.traditional: What have I to do with thee?
notes.note: The Greek is a compressed idiom, literally “What to me and to you?”, familiar from the Greek Old Testament. It usually puts distance between speaker and hearer: “Why are you involving me?” Some translators instead take it as “What concern is that to you and to me?”, which makes the shortage neither person’s business. In both readings Jesus declines to act at once without rebuking her.

In Greek this was an ordinary and courteous way to address a woman, without the harshness the bare word has in modern English. Jesus uses it again to his mother from the cross (19:26). It is nonetheless an unusual way for a son to address his mother, and many interpreters think it signals some distance. No English term captures both the courtesy and the reserve, so the plain word is kept.

notes.traditional: two or three firkins / twenty or thirty gallons
notes.note: The Greek says each jar held “two or three measures”. The measure in question was a liquid unit of roughly 39 litres, or about nine to ten gallons. The six jars together held somewhere around 120 to 180 gallons (about 450 to 700 litres). Stone vessels were preferred for purification water because, in Jewish practice, stone was not considered liable to ritual impurity.

notes.traditional: governor of the feast / master of the feast
notes.note: The Greek word is rare. It may mean the head servant in charge of the dining arrangements, or a guest chosen to preside over the feast. His free manner with the bridegroom in verse 10 fits a presiding guest somewhat better, but the matter is not settled. “Master of the banquet” leaves both possibilities open.

notes.traditional: have well drunk / have drunk freely
notes.note: The verb means to become intoxicated, and that is its regular sense in the period. Many English versions soften it to “have drunk freely”. The man is quoting a general rule of thumb about hosts and is not describing the state of these particular guests. The Greek says simply “when they are drunk”; “the guests” is supplied for clarity.

John uses two different words that English versions usually both translate “temple”. The word here means the whole sacred complex with its outer courts, where the trading took place. The word in verses 19–21 means the sanctuary building itself. “Temple courts” here and “temple” there keeps the distinction a Greek reader would have heard.

notes.traditional: drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen
notes.note: The Greek can mean that Jesus drove out all the animals (“all of them, both the sheep and the cattle”), or that he drove out all the traders together with their animals. The grammar slightly favours the first reading, but “all” is masculine and could refer to the people. The rendering follows the first reading and leaves the second possible.

notes.phrase: Zeal for your house will consume me.
notes.traditional: The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up
notes.note: The quotation is from Psalm 69:9 (68:10 in the Greek numbering), a psalm of a righteous sufferer that early Christians often applied to Jesus. The psalm has “has consumed me”; John’s wording has the future “will consume”, which readers have long taken as pointing forward to Jesus’s death.

The Greek says simply “the Jews”, as in verses 6 and 13. Here and in verse 20 those who demand Jesus’s credentials for acting in the temple are best understood as the authorities responsible for it, not the Jewish people as a whole, to whom Jesus and his disciples belonged. John often uses the term in this narrower way. Scholars are divided on how to translate it: some prefer “Judeans” throughout, while others keep “the Jews” everywhere.

notes.traditional: Forty and six years was this temple in building
notes.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the Jerusalem temple around 20–19 BC, which places this exchange at about AD 27–28. Work on the wider complex continued until the 60s AD, only a few years before the Romans destroyed it. The Greek could describe a completed phase of building or construction still in progress.

The same Greek verb appears in verse 23 and verse 24: many “trusted” in Jesus, but Jesus did not “trust” himself to them. Traditional versions have “believed” and then “commit” or “entrust”, which hides the deliberate echo. The verb covers both believing and trusting; it is rendered “believed” in verses 11 and 22 and “trusted” here so that the echo can be heard.

candidates.reason: It names the whole temple complex as distinct from ναός, the sanctuary, and the two need a fixed pair of English renderings across the Gospels and Acts.
It needs a decision between “temple” and “sanctuary” that holds across the Gospels, Paul’s body-as-temple passages and Revelation, in contrast with ἱερόν.
It is a key term in John and recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts, where older versions vary between “sign” and “miracle”.
It is used both for raising a building or person up and for resurrection, and the active/passive choice (“rose” or “was raised”) should be consistent across the New Testament.
